## The schedule that said "quarterly" and the review that never ran

Six weeks after the Select conversation that closed out the last module, you're back with your
Quality Analyst and your systems administrator for what's supposed to be a short status check.
Your systems administrator opens with something close to triumph: "All three families are built.
Every eQMS (electronic quality-management system) account across all three sites is tied to a
named role now, not a shared login. Every CAPA (corrective and preventive action), document-
control, and audit-log change gets logged — who, what, when. And I confirmed the data center
that hosts the eQMS has backup power and fire suppression, in writing." He slides a one-page
summary across the table, visibly proud of it, and he's earned the right to be — six weeks ago
his answer to "who has access" was "the usual people."

You read the summary, and one line catches your eye: *account access reviewed quarterly, owned
by [him], first review due last month.* You ask the obvious follow-up: "Did that first review
happen?"

He pauses. "It's on the calendar. I haven't actually run it yet — I was heads-down building the
other two pieces." Your Quality Analyst, sitting across from both of you, says nothing yet, but
you can see her making a note. That pause is the whole reason this module exists: building a
control and having it actually work are two different facts, and nobody in the room — including
the person who built it — is the right person to confirm which one is true here.

## Why this step exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure Implement and Assess together are built to prevent, and it's the natural
next failure after Categorize and Select: a team picks the right controls, on paper, sized to
the right impact level — and then either never actually builds them, or builds them and takes
the builder's word that they work. A control that exists only as a line item in a selection
table protects nobody. A control the builder insists works, checked by nobody else, protects
exactly as much as the builder's own blind spots allow — which is usually quite a bit less than
the builder believes, for the same reason nobody proofreads their own writing well.

You already know this exact two-step discipline from ITSM (IT service management), just under
different names. **Implement** is change implementation — actually deploying the change you
approved, not just approving it. **Assess** is the step right after it that a mature change
practice never skips: validation and testing, ideally run by someone who wasn't the one who
built the change, before anyone calls it done. A change record that says "implemented" with no
post-implementation review attached is exactly as incomplete as your systems administrator's
one-page summary was the moment you asked about the review date. Nobody accepts "I built it" as
proof it works in a change process you'd defend to an auditor; the same standard applies here.

## The rule in plain English

**Implement** means two things happen, not one: Lakeshore actually builds the control families
Select chose, *and* writes down how each one actually operates — who owns it, what triggers it,
what it produces as evidence. A control nobody wrote the mechanics of is a control nobody can
later prove was ever real.

**Assess** means someone who didn't build the control checks whether it's actually doing what it
was built to do — not whether it exists, but whether it's "operating as intended" and
"producing the desired outcome." Those are RMF's (Risk Management Framework's) own words, and
they're doing real work: a control can exist, be documented beautifully, and still not yet be
proven to work, the way your systems administrator's access-review schedule exists and is
documented and still hasn't actually run once.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Ch. 2 (Figure 2 framing — Implement) | "...Chapter Two" | U.S. government work, public domain, safe to quote verbatim. States that Implement means building the controls *and* describing how they're employed within the system and its environment of operation. | Actually configuring account access, audit logging, and the physical/environmental confirmation for the eQMS — and writing down how each one works. |
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Ch. 2 (Figure 2 framing — Assess) | "...Chapter Two" | Same tier. States that Assess means determining whether the controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcomes. | The QA's independent check of all three control families, six weeks after they were built. |

## The actual text

Implement's one-line action, quoted verbatim from `sources/nist/sp-800-37r2-excerpt.md` (part
of the Figure 2 passage already quoted in full in `risk-frameworks-side-by-side` — this is the
one line this module actually acts on):

> Implement the controls and describe how the controls are employed within the system and
> its environment of operation.

Two separate obligations live inside that one sentence, and it's easy to read only the first
half. "Implement the controls" is the build. "Describe how the controls are employed within the
system and its environment of operation" is a documentation requirement sitting right next to
it, not an afterthought — RMF doesn't consider a control implemented just because it exists; it
has to be described well enough that someone who didn't build it could understand how it
actually operates.

Assess's one-line action, quoted verbatim from the same excerpt:

> Assess the controls to determine if the controls are implemented correctly, operating as
> intended, and producing the desired outcomes with respect to satisfying the security and
> privacy requirements.

Three separate questions live inside that sentence too, and they're not the same question asked
three times: *implemented correctly* (built the way it was designed), *operating as intended*
(actually running, not just configured and forgotten), and *producing the desired outcomes*
(the thing it's supposed to catch, it actually catches). A control can pass the first test and
fail the third — built correctly, technically running, but never yet exercised against a real
case, which is exactly where your systems administrator's access review sits this week.

## What actually got built

Walk through what "implement" meant for each of the three families Select chose last module,
concretely, not just named again.

**Account and identity management.** Every eQMS account across Lakeshore's three sites is now
tied to a named individual and a specific role — no shared logins, no "the usual people." New
access requires a documented request and an approval step before the account is created. On top
of that, your systems administrator owns a quarterly access-review cycle: every quarter, he
pulls the full access list per site, checks it against who currently holds each role, and signs
off that it still matches. That's the control as designed. The documentation piece — RMF's
"describe how the controls are employed" requirement — means this isn't just a verbal
understanding between you and him; it's written down who owns the review, what triggers it
(the calendar date, not a complaint), and what it produces (a signed, dated reconciliation per
site).

**Audit and logging.** The eQMS's built-in audit-logging feature is turned on across all three
sites, configured to capture every change to a CAPA record, a document-control record, or an
audit-log entry itself — who made the change, what field changed, and when. It's not enough that
the feature exists in the software; it has to actually be switched on, and the written
description has to say what fields it captures and that the log itself is retained for at least
as long as the records it's logging changes to, so the log can't quietly be shorter-lived than
the evidence it's supposed to protect.

**Physical and environmental protection.** Wherever the eQMS's underlying infrastructure
actually sits — a question the last module left open and this one answers by confirming, not
assuming — your systems administrator obtained written confirmation that the hosting facility
has the basics: backup power, fire suppression, and controlled physical access to the server
room itself. That confirmation is now a dated document Lakeshore holds, not a assumption nobody
ever checked.

All three of those are real, specific builds — not a restatement of the family names from last
module. That's what distinguishes "implemented" from "selected."

## The independent assessment

Here's where the scene that opened this lesson actually matters. Your systems administrator
built all three families. That makes him the wrong person to confirm they work — not because
you doubt his honesty, but for the same reason this curriculum already established once,
in `designing-an-internal-audit-program`: an auditor can't check their own work. The same rule
applies here, one layer removed from an audit: whoever builds a control isn't the person who
gets to declare it effective.

So you hand the assessment to your Quality Analyst — she didn't build any of the three families,
which clears her against that same independence test. She checks each one against RMF's three
questions: implemented correctly, operating as intended, producing the desired outcome.

**Physical and environmental protection** clears all three. The written confirmation exists, is
dated, and matches what the facility actually provides.

**Audit and logging** clears all three. She spot-checks the log against a handful of recent
CAPA and document-control edits and confirms it's actually capturing who, what, and when for
each one — not just configured, but producing real entries.

**Account and identity management** is where she stops. The process is implemented correctly —
the account structure, the request-and-approval step, and the quarterly review schedule are all
real and documented, exactly as described. But the first scheduled review never actually ran;
its due date already passed by the time she assessed it. That means Lakeshore has no evidence
yet that the review actually catches what it's designed to catch — a stale account, a role that
changed without access following it, an account that should have been revoked. The control
exists and is documented. It has not yet been exercised, and "producing the desired outcomes" is
exactly the test it hasn't had the chance to pass.

That is the one concrete deficiency this module's assessment produces: **the quarterly eQMS
access-review control is implemented and documented, but has not yet been exercised on its first
scheduled cycle.** Not a vague "access controls need work" — a specific, dated, named gap. This
is also exactly what Assess is supposed to do. Finding this is the process working, not the
process failing; the whole reason an independent assessment happens before an authorization
decision is so a gap like this surfaces here; carrying it forward honestly, not hiding it, is
this module's actual job.

## What a reviewer would actually look for

What a competent reviewer — your CIO, your QA acting as assessor, or you yourself revisiting
this later — wants to find for each control family is the same four things: a written
description of how the control actually operates, evidence it was actually configured (not just
designed), evidence someone independent of the builder checked it, and an honest statement of
what that check found, including anything short of fully working. A bad answer sounds like "the
administrator says it's all set." A good answer sounds like the walkthrough above: three
families, each checked by someone who didn't build it, two confirmed working and one named
honestly as not yet proven.

## Common traps

**"It's built, so it's done."** Implement and Assess are two separate steps for a reason — a
control that exists is not the same fact as a control that works, and RMF's own language
("operating as intended," "producing the desired outcomes") exists specifically to stop a team
from treating "we configured it" as the finish line.

**"The person who built it is the best person to confirm it works."** Backwards, on purpose.
The person who built it knows it best, which is exactly why they're the worst-positioned person
to notice what they missed. Independence isn't a formality here — it's the only way a gap like
an unrun access review actually gets found instead of assumed away.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask for the written "how it operates" description before you believe a control is
  implemented**, not just a verbal confirmation it exists. If nobody can hand you that
  description, Implement's own documentation half hasn't actually happened yet.
- **Never let the builder self-certify.** Whoever configured a control names someone else — your
  QA, a peer, an outside reviewer if nobody internal clears the independence test — to check it,
  the same release valve `designing-an-internal-audit-program` already built for exactly this
  staffing problem.
- **Treat "implemented but not yet exercised" as a real, nameable finding, not a technicality.**
  A quarterly review that hasn't run its first cycle yet is not the same fact as a review that
  ran and found nothing wrong — don't let anyone round the first up to the second.
- **Expect an assessment to find something.** A first-pass assessment that clears every control
  with zero findings is itself worth a second look — it's more often a sign nobody looked hard
  enough than a sign everything is actually perfect.
- **Keep the finding specific enough to act on.** "Account management needs attention" doesn't
  give the next module anything to authorize around. "The quarterly review is documented but its
  first cycle hasn't run yet" does.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator asks why writing down "how" the access-review control works matters, since the control itself — the quarterly schedule — already exists. What do you tell him?

Because Implement's own one-line action requires both things: building the control *and*
describing how it's employed within the system and its environment of operation. A control that
exists only in someone's head, or as a verbal understanding between two people, can't be checked
by anyone independent, can't survive him changing roles or leaving, and can't be assessed against
what it was supposed to do. The written description is what makes the control real enough for
someone else to verify — which is exactly what happens next, in Assess.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Could your systems administrator have assessed his own account-and-identity-management build himself, to save time, since he's the one who understands it best?

No. The same independence rule this curriculum already established for internal audits —
the person checking the work can't be the person who did the work — applies here. Understanding
a control best is exactly what makes its builder the least likely person to notice what it's
missing; that's not a knock on his competence, it's just how blind spots work. The assessment has
to go to someone who didn't build it, which is why it went to the QA.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The assessment found a real gap — the access review hasn't run its first cycle yet. Does that mean Lakeshore failed Implement and Assess?

No — it means they worked. Assess exists specifically to surface a gap like this *before* anyone
decides whether to authorize the eQMS for use, not to rubber-stamp whatever got built. An
assessment that found nothing wrong on the very first pass would actually be more worth
questioning than one that found something concrete and specific. The failure would be building
the control, skipping an independent check, and finding out about the unrun review some other
way — from an assessor, or from the gap actually being exploited.
:::

## Where this goes next

Implement built the three control families and wrote down how each one works. Assess checked
all three independently and found two working and one real, specific, open item: the quarterly
access review, implemented and documented, not yet exercised on its first cycle. Someone now has
to decide what to do with that open item before the eQMS goes live — accept it as a named,
time-bound risk, or hold go-live until it's closed. That decision, and the ongoing monitoring
plan that follows it, is `authorize-and-monitor`.
